faq.a: The hippocampus is a curved structure deep in each temporal lobe. It is vital for forming new memories of facts and events and for linking them together, before they are stored more widely in the cortex.
Short-term or working memory holds a small amount of information for seconds to minutes, like a number you are about to dial. Most people can hold only around four to seven items at once.

faq.q: What happens to nerve cells when you learn?
faq.a: The connections between them, called synapses, change. Nerve cells that fire together become better at signalling each other, so the pattern is easier to trigger again.
asks: Tell me about the links strengthening

faq.a: Connections that are not used tend to weaken, new memories can interfere with old ones, and some things are never stored properly because we did not pay attention.

faq.q: Why does practice help you remember?
faq.a: Each time you recall or practise something, the connections behind it are strengthened, so the memory becomes easier to find. Spreading practice over days works better than cramming.

facts: The hippocampus is named from the Greek for seahorse because of its shape.
Memories are consolidated, or strengthened, partly during sleep.
